notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Isaiah 65 from the sources I was able to access. The research is organized verse by verse, with the tradition or source clearly noted for each point.

---

## Isaiah 65 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overall Structure

The chapter is widely understood as God's answer to the prayer of the remnant in Isaiah 63:7–64:12. Commentators across traditions see three main sections:

- **vv. 1–7** — God exposes shallow repentance and self-righteous hypocrisy among His people.
- **vv. 8–16** — A contrast between true servants (blessed) and false servants (judged).
- **vv. 17–25** — Promise of new heavens, a new earth, and a transformed creation.

(EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

---

### v. 1: "I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me…"

**The key interpretive question is who the speaker addresses.** There are two major readings:

- **Gentile-calling reading:** Paul in Romans 10:20 applies this verse to the calling of the Gentiles. The Pulpit Commentary states that "the application of the text by St. Paul… will be felt by all believers in inspiration to preclude the interpretation which supposes Israel to be the subject of v. 1." God's mercy overflows upon those outside the covenant. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- **Israel-reading:** Ellicott notes that "taking the text as it stands, the most natural interpretation… seems to be that Jehovah speaks to the same people in Isaiah 65:1-2, and that both alike speak of indifference and hardness." The meaning is that God was ready to answer Israel despite their indifference, and Israel "has sunk to the level of the heathen." On this view, Paul's use of the LXX is a free application, analogous to his use of Hosea in Romans 9. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **Calvin** strongly affirms the Gentile-calling view, saying the Prophet "shews that God has good reason for rejecting and casting off the Jews… he will have another people which formerly was no people." He says God anticipated the Gentiles by grace: "they brought no merit or excellence as an inducement to God." (Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-65.html)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Applies verse 1 "TO GENTILES who were willing to yield themselves, in faith, to the lordship of Jesus Christ." (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/isaiah-65.html)

---

### v. 2: "All day long I have held out My hands to an obstinate people…"

- **All agree** this verse addresses Israel. Paul applies it in Romans 10:21: "to Israel he says, 'All day long I have stretched out My hands to a disobedient and contrary people.'" (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

- **"Held out My hands"** — The Pulpit Commentary says this gesture is "not exactly in prayer, but in expostulation" (cf. Proverbs 1:24). It signifies God's persistent, patient appeal over centuries. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- **"Who walk in the wrong path, who follow their own imaginations"** — EnduringWord notes that walking "according to their own thoughts" is the very definition of a rebellious people. Trusting our own wisdom puts us among the rebellious. This echoes Judges 17:6 and 21:25 ("everyone did what was right in his own eyes") and Proverbs 14:12. (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

- **Calvin** says God "accuses the Jews, and complains of their ingratitude and rebellion… The Jews conducted themselves proudly and insolently toward God, as if they had been elected through their own merit." (Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-65.html)

---

### v. 3: "…sacrificing in the gardens and burning incense on altars of brick"

- **Gardens:** Both Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary identify these as sites of idolatrous worship, particularly of Astarte (the Dea Syra), involving ritual sensualism in groves and garden precincts. Ellicott notes this was common under Ahaz (cf. Isaiah 1:29). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm; Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- **"Altars of brick"** — Literally "upon the bricks." The Pulpit Commentary suggests incense was burned on the tiled or bricked roofs of houses, as in Jeremiah 19:13 and Zephaniah 1:5, where incense was offered to "the host of heaven." Brick altars are not otherwise attested; proper altars under the Law were of earth or unhewn stone (Exodus 20:24–25). (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- **Constable** notes: "Gardens were unauthorized places for sacrificing, and bricks were unauthorized materials for an altar." The people provoked God by offering sacrifices "in ways that were unacceptable to Him." (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

---

### v. 4: "sitting among the graves, spending nights in secret places, eating the meat of pigs…"

- **Sitting among the graves / spending nights in secret places:** The Pulpit Commentary identifies these as necromantic practices — seeking to raise the dead for prophecies, or sleeping in crypts to receive dream-oracles. Ellicott notes Jerome observed that men slept in crypts of the temple of Æsculapius hoping for visions of the future. Both sources identify these as violations of ceremonial law regarding contact with the dead (Numbers 19:11). (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **Eating swine's flesh:** Both Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary agree this was not mere dietary defiance but participation in sacrificial meals. Swine were sacrificial animals in Egypt, Phoenicia, Greece, and Rome — likely at sacrifices to Baal or Astarte. Ellicott notes that "no reference to swine has been found in any cuneiform inscriptions," so this likely points to Canaanite (not Babylonian) idolatry. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm; Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- **"Polluted broth":** Broth from unclean animals consumed in sacrificial feasts connected with heathen mysteries. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

---

### v. 5: "'Keep to yourself; do not come near me, for I am holier than you!' Such people are smoke in My nostrils…"

- **The shocking self-righteousness:** The people steeped in the sins described in vv. 3–4 nonetheless claimed superior holiness. Ellicott explains this as boasting of "initiation into heathen mysteries" which supposedly conferred a holiness unavailable to ordinary Israelites faithful to Yahweh. The Hebrew is literally "I am holy to thee" — i.e., one you may not approach. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **Spurgeon** preached a sermon titled "Self-Righteousness — A Smouldering Heap of Rubbish" on this text. He described how "self-righteous men, like foxes, have many tricks and schemes. They condemn in other people what they consider to be very excusable in themselves." He also targeted religious hypocrites: "Those who come with the language of repentance but without the spirit of it, are sometimes the most self-righteous of all, for they say 'I am all right because I am not self-righteous.'" Spurgeon added: "This weed of self-righteousness will grow on any dunghill. No heap of rubbish is too rotten for the accursed toadstool of proud self to grow upon." (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/ — quoting Spurgeon)

- **"Smoke in My nostrils, a fire that burns all day":** The Pulpit Commentary says the heathenized Jews are "fuel for the wrath of God, which kindles a fire wherein they burn continually." Ellicott similarly says they are "already as those who are being consumed in the fire of the Divine wrath." (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

---

### v. 6: "Behold, it is written before Me: I will not keep silent, but I will repay…"

- **"It is written before Me":** All commentators see this as the heavenly register, God's book of remembrance (cf. Psalm 56:8; Malachi 3:16; Revelation 20:12). Ellicott says: "Men took the long-suffering of God as if it indicated forgetfulness. They are told that He will at last requite the impenitent 'into their very bosom.'" (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm; Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- **"Into their laps"** (bosom): Refers to the fold of the cloak where gifts were received — full, personal recompense. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

---

### v. 7: "both for your iniquities and for those of your fathers…"

- **Accumulated guilt:** The judgment is not only for one generation's sin but for the accumulated iniquities of fathers who "burned incense on the mountains." This refers to the long-standing sin of high-place worship (cf. 2 Kings 17:11; Hosea 4:13; Ezekiel 6:13). Ellicott says the worship at high places was "practically a 'blasphemy' or 'reproach' against Him." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm; Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- **"Measure into their laps full payment":** The Pulpit Commentary notes "first of all" — God will deal with their sin before turning to promise blessing. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

---

### v. 8: "As the new wine is found in a cluster of grapes… 'Do not destroy it, for it contains a blessing'…"

- **The grape-cluster simile:** The Pulpit Commentary explains: as when even a single cluster of grapes is found on a vine-stem, the vine-dressers say "Spare that stem," so God will not destroy those stocks in His vineyard that show even small promise of good fruit. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- **"Destroy it not":** Ellicott notes this phrase heads Psalms 57–59 as a tune direction — it was likely "a popular vintage song, and therefore doubly apt for the prophet's purpose." The thought is that as one good cluster spares an otherwise fruitless vine, so God spares a sinful nation for the sake of the righteous remnant (cf. Genesis 18:23–33). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **EnduringWord:** "God preserves a faithful remnant — good grapes in a corrupt cluster — and for their sake shows blessing and restoration to the whole nation, just as He would have spared Sodom for five righteous people." (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

- **Constable:** "Yahweh promised not to destroy the whole nation (cluster of grapes), but just the sinners among them (the bad grapes)." (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

---

### v. 9: "I will bring forth descendants from Jacob, and heirs from Judah; My elect will possess My mountains…"

- **Jacob and Judah:** Ellicott says these "are used to represent respectively the remnants of the two kingdoms that had been carried into captivity." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **"My mountains":** The mountainous terrain of Palestine — not just Zion but "every hill in Canaan was a sharer in a derived sanctity." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Sees "an inheritor of My mountains" as pointing ultimately to the Christ (cf. Psalm 2:8; Hebrews 1:2). But the elect servants share in the inheritance. (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/isaiah-65.html)

---

### v. 10: "Sharon will become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a resting place for herds…"

- **Sharon:** The rich coastal plain from Joppa to Carmel. Ellicott notes the LXX and Josephus render it "the plain" or "the woodland." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **Valley of Achor:** Traditionally connected with the sin of Achan (Joshua 7:24–26), a valley near Jericho. Ellicott sees these two locations as representing the western (Sharon) and eastern (Achor) boundaries of the land — the whole territory will be restored. Constable agrees: the faithful "would inhabit the fertile western coastal plain and the barren eastern area west of Jericho, in other words, the whole land." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- **"For My people who seek Me":** The Pulpit Commentary notes this limits the promise to true seekers, excluding the hypocritical idolaters. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

---

### v. 11: "But you who forsake the LORD… who set a table for Fortune and fill bowls of mixed wine for Destiny"

- **"Fortune" (Gad) and "Destiny" (Meni):** Ellicott identifies Gad as the planet Jupiter, worshipped as "the greater fortune," the giver of good luck. Meni is probably Venus as the "lesser fortune." The LXX renders Gad as "the demon" or "genius." The "table" points to ritual feasts (lectisternia). Constable adds that these "may have been what became identified later with the planets Jupiter ('the greater luck') and Venus ('the lesser luck'), or with the sun and moon." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- **"Forget My holy mountain":** Means either literally forgetting Zion while exiled (Psalm 137:5) or neglecting the Temple for heathen worship. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

---

### v. 12: "I will destine you for the sword… because I called and you did not answer…"

- **"Destine" (number):** A wordplay on the name Meni ("Destiny"). The Pulpit Commentary says: "Therefore will I number you (apportion you) — a play upon the name of M'ni." Those who trusted Fortune and Destiny would have their true destiny appointed by God — the sword. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- **The sin of not answering:** EnduringWord highlights that refusing to respond to God's conviction is worse than falling into sin through weakness — "it is bad enough to be speeding down the highway; it is worse to ignore the flashing red lights in your rearview mirror." (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

---

### vv. 13–14: "My servants will eat, but you will go hungry… My servants will rejoice, but you will be put to shame."

- **Series of contrasts:** Ellicott notes the form of punishment is determined by the sin — those who feasted at idol tables will hunger and thirst; those who abstained will have joy. He compares the language to Luke 6:20–26 (the Beatitudes and woes). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- The Pulpit Commentary sees both a literal and spiritual fulfilment: the religious exiles prospered upon return (Ezra 3:11–13) while the irreligious who stayed in Babylon suffered; but also, "God's servants at all times and in all places would be sustained with spiritual food." (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- Garner-Howes notes: "The Lord's true servants will be adequately supplied with food and drink… while the wicked and rebellious will hunger and thirst." (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/isaiah-65.html)

---

### v. 15: "You will leave behind your name as a curse for My chosen ones… to His servants He will give another name."

- **Name as a curse:** The idea is that the name of the judged becomes a formula of imprecation — "The LORD make you like…" (cf. Jeremiah 29:22; Numbers 5:21; Zechariah 8:13). (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm; Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

- **"Another name":** Constable clarifies this is "not a replacement of all Israel by the church, but a replacement of all who depended on formal worship… by those who genuinely loved and obeyed God." The "another name" echoes Isaiah 62:2 and Revelation 2:17; 3:12. (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

---

### v. 16: "Whoever invokes a blessing in the land will do so by the God of truth…"

- **"The God of truth"** — Literally "the God of the Amen." Ellicott says this implies "the prophet had entered into the inner meaning of what was to most men only a liturgical formula." In Revelation 3:14 Christ is called "the Amen, the Faithful and True Witness." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **EnduringWord:** The God of truth is "the God who says 'amen' to all his promises, affirming their reality and his trustworthiness to keep them" (Motyer). The judgment on false servants and blessing on true servants is necessary so that God is shown to be the God of truth. (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

- **"Former troubles will be forgotten":** This transitional phrase leads into the great promise of the new creation. (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

---

### vv. 17–25: The New Heavens, New Earth, and the Millennial Question

**This is the most debated section across Protestant traditions.**

#### v. 17: "For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered…"

- **Traditional Christian reading:** This is the ultimate eschatological hope. Ellicott notes the thought reappears in 2 Peter 3:13, Revelation 21:1, Acts 3:21 ("restitution of all things"), and Romans 8:19. "The 'former things,' the sin and sorrow of the past, shall then fade away from the memory of God's people, absorbed in the abounding and everlasting joy." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **The millennial/eternal state distinction (Premillennial):** EnduringWord (David Guzik, a premillennial charismatic teacher) argues that Isaiah "is in the prophetic habit of switching quickly from one time frame to another, speaking of the eternal state in Isaiah 65:17, and of the millennial earth in Isaiah 65:20–25." He bases this on: (a) v. 17 says the former shall not be remembered, but in the millennium there will be remembrance (Ezekiel 40–46 temple rituals); (b) vv. 20–25 describe conditions with death, birth, and sinners — impossible in the eternal state (Revelation 21:4 says no more death). Therefore v. 17 is the eternal state, and vv. 20–25 describe the millennial kingdom. (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

- **Constable (Dispensational):** Similarly argues: "Isaiah described the future in general terms as 'a new heaven and a new earth.' In the New Testament, we have further particularization… the making of all things new for those in Christ presently (Galatians 2:20), the millennial kingdom (Revelation 20:4–6), and the 'eternal state' (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1). Thus Isaiah's use of 'new heavens and a new earth' is not identical with the Apostle John's." Most of vv. 17–25 describes "God's renovation of creation during the Millennium." (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- **Amillennial/Spiritual reading:** The Pulpit Commentary, representing an older Anglican perspective, sees the whole passage describing one glorious future state of the church, but acknowledges a tension: "Isaiah's picture, according to Delitzsch, represents the millennial state, not the final condition of the redeemed; but this trait — the absence of all weeping — can only be literally true of the final state." Delitzsch himself (quoted by Constable) said: "The Old Testament prophet was not yet able to distinguish from one another the things which the author of the Apocalypse separates into distinct periods." (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** States that the "newness" involved "is NOT that of something ENTIRELY DIFFERENT, but involves a 'renewing or restoring'" — linking it to the millennial kingdom under Messiah. (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/isaiah-65.html)

- **Calvin/Reformed:** The excerpts available indicate Calvin read this promise as fulfilled in the Gospel church — the new creation inaugurated spiritually through Christ. His commentary on v. 17 was not fully fetched, but earlier Calvin material shows he saw the new heavens and earth as Gospel-era renewal. (Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-65.html)

#### vv. 18–19: "I will create Jerusalem to be a joy… The sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in her."

- Ellicott notes that from the prophet's standpoint, "the earthly city, transformed and transfigured, occupies the central place in the new creation. In the New Testament we note the transfer of the promise to the unseen eternal city, the Jerusalem which is above (Galatians 4:26; Revelation 21:10)." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- Constable: "God Himself would also rejoice in the new city and in the new people… Weeping and crying would end in that new city (Revelation 21:4)." (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- **Spurgeon** preached on vv. 17–19 in a sermon titled "God Rejoicing in the New Creation," emphasizing the present spiritual joy believers have as "part thereof" now. (Spurgeon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/god-rejoicing-in-the-new-creation)

#### v. 20: "No longer will a nursing infant live but a few days… the youth will die at a hundred years…"

- **Key debate:** This verse describes death and sin still present — which premillennial interpreters take as proof this describes the millennial kingdom, not the eternal state. EnduringWord: "There will be death in the millennial earth, but in the transformed biology and ecology of the world under the reign of Jesus Christ, people will live incredibly longer, as they did in the days before the flood." (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

- Ellicott observes: "The noticeable fact is that sin is thought of as not altogether extinct — as still appearing, though under altered conditions, even in the restored Jerusalem." He sees a return to "the traditional longevity of the prediluvian and patriarchal age." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- Constable: "This prediction requires the conditions of an earthly city, where babies are born and older people die (even though the average lifespan is to be much prolonged)." (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- The Pulpit Commentary acknowledges the difficulty: "What is most remarkable in the description is that death and sin are represented as still continuing. Death was spoken of as 'swallowed up in victory' in one of the earlier descriptions of Messiah's kingdom (Isaiah 25:8)." (Pulpit: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/65.htm)

#### vv. 21–23: "They will build houses and dwell in them… they will not labor in vain…"

- **Social justice restored:** The curse of Deuteronomy 28:30 (building houses others inhabit, planting vineyards others eat) is reversed. Constable: "Life will not be futile or frustrating, labor will amount to something." (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- EnduringWord emphasizes that in the millennium, perfect justice will reign, and Satan will be bound (Revelation 20:1–3), preventing his destructive mischief. (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

- **"As the days of a tree":** Ellicott: "We may think of the cedars of Lebanon or the oaks of Bashan as furnishing the prophet with the ideal standard of longevity." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- **Children born:** EnduringWord notes this is evidence of the millennial (not eternal) state: "In the eternal state, we neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels of God in heaven (Matthew 22:30)." (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

#### v. 24: "Even before they call, I will answer, and while they are still speaking, I will hear."

- Ellicott: "In man's experience of men, often… there is an interval between prayer and the answer. In the new Jerusalem the two would be simultaneous, or the answer would anticipate the prayer." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm)

- Constable: "Perfect communication with God will be another blessing of this peaceable kingdom. Christians already enjoy good communication with Him (Matthew 6:8; 1 John 5:14–15), but in the future it will be even better." (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- EnduringWord notes that though this intimacy will be widely enjoyed in the millennium, "this does not mean that everyone on the millennial earth will be saved" — Satan will find willing rebels at the millennium's end (Revelation 20:7–9). (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

#### v. 25: "The wolf and the lamb will feed together… the lion will eat straw like the ox, but the food of the serpent will be dust."

- **Parallel to Isaiah 11:6–9:** This is the classic picture of peace in the animal kingdom under Messiah's reign. (EnduringWord: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-65/)

- **The serpent eating dust:** Ellicott connects this to Genesis 3:14 — the curse on the serpent. "Even the serpent… shall find food in the dust in which he crawls, and shall be no longer a destroyer. The condition of the ideal Paradise should be restored." Constable notes this has "only been fulfilled figuratively so far — snakes do not literally feed on dust now but on plants and animals." (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/65.htm; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

- **"They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain":** The glorious conclusion. Constable summarizes Isaiah's four new things for Jerusalem: joy replacing weeping, longevity replacing sorrow, answered prayer replacing silence, and universal peace replacing violence. (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-65.html)

---

## Summary of Protestant Tradition Differences

### The Millennial Debate (vv. 17–25)

| Position | Reading of Isaiah 65:17–25 |
|---|---|
| **Premillennial** (EnduringWord/Pentecostal-Charismatic, Garner-Howes Baptist, Constable/Dispensational) | v. 17 = eternal state; vv. 20–25 = millennial kingdom on earth, with death, birth, long lifespans, and lingering sin. Jesus rules personally from Jerusalem. |
| **Amillennial** (implied in Calvin, some Reformed) | The "new heavens and new earth" describe the present Gospel age spiritually, or a blended picture of the final state. The Church is the New Jerusalem. |
| **Postmillennial** (not directly represented in the sources found) | The millennium is brought about progressively through the Church's influence before Christ returns. Isaiah 65 describes this golden age. |

### v. 1 — Gentiles or Israel?

| Position | Reading |
|---|---|
| **Traditional Protestant / Pauline** (Pulpit, Calvin, Baptist, EnduringWord) | v. 1 speaks of the calling of the Gentiles, as Paul applies it in Romans 10:20. |
| **Critical/Academic** (Ellicott) | v. 1 originally referred to wayward Israel; Paul's use is a free application, not the original meaning. |

### The "Another Name" (v. 15)

- Some see this as the name "Christian" (Acts 11:26) or the new name in Revelation.
- Constable cautions against seeing a replacement of Israel by the Church; rather it is the replacement of formalists by genuine worshippers within the people of God.
